topic: Vectors and Analytic Geometry in Space

nodes.label: Three-Dimensional Cartesian Coordinates and Spheres
nodes.explanation: Assumes university entry background in 2D Cartesian geometry, completing the square, the Pythagorean theorem, and basic trigonometry. Establishes the right-handed 3D rectangular coordinate system ℝ³ (x-, y-, and z-axes oriented by the right-hand rule), the three coordinate planes (xy-, yz-, and xz-planes), the eight octants, and orthogonal projections of a point (x, y, z) onto coordinate axes and coordinate planes. Derives the 3D Euclidean distance formula d(P, Q) = √((x_2 − x_1)² + (y_2 − y_1)² + (z_2 − z_1)²) via two successive applications of the Pythagorean theorem, together with the midpoint formula and distance from a point to a coordinate plane or axis. Develops standard and expanded equations of spheres (x − h)² + (y − k)² + (z − l)² = r², using triple completing-the-square to identify centers, radii, single-point spheres, and empty loci, and trains describing simple 3D coordinate regions such as balls, spherical shells, slabs, and half-spaces via inequalities. Enables the learner to plot and visualize points, regions, and spheres in ℝ³ and extract geometric parameters from quadratic sphere equations. Leaves 3D vectors, planes, general surfaces, and non-Cartesian coordinates to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Vectors in ℝ³, Components, and Algebraic Operations
nodes.explanation: Builds on 3D Cartesian coordinates (prior exposure to 2D elementary vectors is helpful background but not required, as 3D vector operations are developed self-containedly here) to establish vectors in three-dimensional space. Represents free 3D vectors geometrically as directed segments invariant under translation and algebraically as ordered triples v = ⟨v_1, v_2, v_3⟩ = v_1 i + v_2 j + v_3 k using the standard unit basis i = ⟨1, 0, 0⟩, j = ⟨0, 1, 0⟩, k = ⟨0, 0, 1⟩, deriving displacement components PQ→ = ⟨x_Q − x_P, y_Q − y_P, z_Q − z_P⟩ and position vectors. Establishes componentwise addition, subtraction, and scalar multiplication, verifies the standard ℝ³ vector-algebra laws, computes magnitude ‖v‖ = √(v_1² + v_2² + v_3²) with ‖kv‖ = |k|‖v‖, normalizes nonzero vectors to unit vectors v / ‖v‖, and characterizes parallel vectors and collinear 3D points via proportional components u = kv (carefully handling zero coordinates). Enables the learner to manipulate 3D vectors algebraically, find unit and scaled direction vectors between spatial points, and test collinearity in ℝ³. Leaves dot, cross, and triple products, 3D lines, and abstract vector-space axioms to later lessons and trees.

nodes.label: Generalized Cylinders and Surfaces of Revolution
nodes.explanation: Builds on 3D Cartesian coordinates and spheres, assuming familiarity with standard 2D conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas) and graphing planar curves, to introduce the first families of curved surfaces in ℝ³. Defines a generalized cylinder as the surface swept by parallel lines (rulings) passing through a planar generating curve (directrix), focusing on equations in ℝ³ that omit one coordinate variable (such as z = x², x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, or y = sin x) whose rulings run parallel to the missing axis—explicitly correcting the common misconception that a cylinder must have a circular cross-section. Develops surfaces of revolution obtained by rotating a planar curve in a coordinate plane around a coordinate axis by replacing the radial distance variable with √(x² + y²), √(x² + z²), or √(y² + z²) as appropriate, identifying when a given equation exhibits rotational symmetry about an axis and recovering its generating profile curve. Enables the learner to recognize, sketch, and write equations for cylinders and surfaces of revolution in ℝ³. Leaves the six general quadric surfaces and full trace classification to the next lesson.

nodes.label: The 3D Dot Product, Direction Cosines, and Projections
nodes.explanation: Builds on vectors in ℝ³, assuming the Law of Cosines, to develop inner-product geometry in space. Defines the 3D dot product u · v = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3, verifies its algebraic properties (symmetry, bilinearity, and v · v = ‖v‖²), and proves u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ via the Law of Cosines on the triangle of u, v, and u − v, deducing the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |u · v| ≤ ‖u‖ ‖v‖, the angle formula, and the orthogonality criterion u · v = 0. Introduces the 3D direction angles (α, β, γ) with the positive coordinate axes and their direction cosines cos α = v_1/‖v‖, cos β = v_2/‖v‖, cos γ = v_3/‖v‖, establishing the fundamental identity cos² α + cos² β + cos² γ = 1 (showing that the triple of direction cosines is precisely the unit vector v / ‖v‖). Develops 3D scalar projection comp_v u = (u · v)/‖v‖, vector projection proj_v u = ((u · v)/(v · v)) v, and the orthogonal decomposition u = proj_v u + (u − proj_v u) (applying it to 3D work W = F · d). Enables the learner to compute angles, verify orthogonality, determine direction cosines, and decompose spatial vectors along arbitrary 3D directions. Leaves cross products, planes, and abstract inner-product spaces to later lessons and trees.

nodes.label: Parametric and Symmetric Equations of Lines in ℝ³
nodes.explanation: Builds on vectors in ℝ³ to formulate and classify lines in three-dimensional space, highlighting the fundamental structural difference from 2D: a single linear equation in x, y, z defines a plane rather than a line. Develops the vector equation r(t) = r_0 + t v, parametric equations (x = x_0 + at, y = y_0 + bt, z = z_0 + ct), and symmetric equations (x − x_0)/a = (y − y_0)/b = (z − z_0)/c when a, b, c ≠ 0—explicitly teaching how zero direction components produce auxiliary constant-coordinate equations (e.g., x = x_0 alongside (y − y_0)/b = (z − z_0)/c) rather than division by zero—and restricts parameters to t ∈ [0, 1] for line segments. Emphasizes non-uniqueness of parametrizations (different base points and scaled direction vectors represent the same line). Trains classifying the relative position of two lines in ℝ³ as coincident, parallel and distinct, intersecting, or skew (non-parallel and non-intersecting, a genuinely 3D phenomenon) by first testing proportionality of direction vectors and otherwise solving the overdetermined 3-equation system in two independent parameters t and s (stressing why distinct parameter names are mandatory to avoid checking only simultaneous collisions). Enables the learner to write, convert, and classify 3D lines and locate exact intersections. Leaves angles with planes, point-to-line distances, and skew-line distances to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Quadric Surfaces and the Method of Traces
nodes.explanation: Builds on cylinders and surfaces of revolution (continuing to use 2D conics and completing the square from earlier background) to classify and sketch second-degree surfaces in ℝ³. Develops the method of traces—intersecting a surface F(x, y, z) = 0 with planes x = k, y = k, and z = k—together with symmetry, intercepts, and domain constraints (identifying values of k that produce empty traces or single points). Systematically analyzes the six standard quadric surfaces: ellipsoids, elliptic paraboloids, hyperbolic paraboloids (saddle surfaces), elliptic cones, hyperboloids of one sheet, and hyperboloids of two sheets, training the learner to distinguish them quickly by term degrees and sign patterns, handle permuted axes (e.g., opening along the y- or x-axis), and apply completing-the-square to identify translated centers or vertices. Contrasts visually confusing pairs such as elliptic cones vs. one- and two-sheet hyperboloids (via the constant term 0 vs. +1 vs. −1 and presence or absence of an empty central gap) and elliptic vs. hyperbolic paraboloids. Enables the learner to classify any axis-aligned quadric equation, determine its traces and orientation, and produce an accurate qualitative 3D sketch. Leaves rotated quadrics requiring eigenvalue diagonalization to Linear Algebra, and multivariable tangent planes to Multivariable Calculus.

nodes.label: The Cross Product, Orientation, and Areas in Space
nodes.explanation: Builds on the 3D dot product and orthogonality to construct the vector (cross) product u × v in ℝ³. Introduces 2×2 and 3×3 determinant expansions purely as a compact computational convention (requiring no prior matrix theory) to define u × v = ⟨u_2 v_3 − u_3 v_2, u_3 v_1 − u_1 v_3, u_1 v_2 − u_2 v_1⟩ via the formal i, j, k cofactor expansion, verifying directly via the dot product that u × v is orthogonal to both u and v. Establishes the algebraic laws: anti-commutativity (u × v = −v × u), bilinearity, u × u = 0, the cyclic basis products i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j, and explicit failure of associativity (demonstrated via (i × i) × j ≠ i × (i × j)). Proves Lagrange's identity ‖u × v‖² = ‖u‖²‖v‖² − (u · v)² by component expansion and deduces the geometric magnitude formula ‖u × v‖ = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ sin θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π) together with the right-hand rule orientation of u × v. Applies the cross product to test parallelism (u × v = 0), compute exact areas of parallelograms (‖u × v‖) and triangles in ℝ³ ((1/2)‖PQ→ × PR→‖), construct vectors perpendicular to two given directions, and interpret physical torque τ = r × F. Enables the learner to compute cross products reliably, find spatial areas and normal vectors, and avoid associativity or sign errors. Leaves triple products and plane equations to the next lessons.

nodes.label: The Scalar Triple Product, Volumes, and Coplanarity
nodes.explanation: Builds on the cross product (and uses the 3D dot product and scalar projection established in its ancestor) to develop the scalar triple product u · (v × w). Derives its 3×3 determinant formula det[u; v; w], proving invariance under cyclic permutations (u · (v × w) = v · (w × u) = w · (u × v)) and sign reversal under swapping any two vectors, while stressing that the parentheses around v × w are structurally forced because (u · v) × w is meaningless. Establishes the geometric volume formula V = |u · (v × w)| for the parallelepiped spanned by u, v, w by multiplying the base area ‖v × w‖ by the perpendicular height |comp_{v×w} u| = |u · (v × w)| / ‖v × w‖, and derives the tetrahedron volume (1/6)|AB→ · (AC→ × AD→)|. Interprets the sign of u · (v × w) as orientation (positive for right-handed triples, negative for left-handed triples) and proves the exact algebraic coplanarity criterion: three vectors are coplanar (equivalently, four points A, B, C, D lie in a common plane) if and only if AB→ · (AC→ × AD→) = 0. Enables the learner to compute volumes of parallelepipeds and tetrahedra, check orientation of 3D frames, and test coplanarity algebraically. Leaves vector triple products to optional enrichment and skew-line distances to the distance synthesis lesson.

nodes.label: Equations of Planes in ℝ³
nodes.explanation: Builds on the cross product (together with the 3D dot product and orthogonality established in its ancestor) to formulate and construct planes in three-dimensional space. Defines a plane uniquely by a point P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0) and a nonzero normal vector n = ⟨a, b, c⟩ via the vector equation n · (r − r_0) = 0, expanding it to the scalar equation a(x − x_0) + b(y − y_0) + c(z − z_0) = 0 and linear Cartesian form ax + by + cz = d, while emphasizing how to read a normal vector directly from the coefficients of any linear equation in x, y, z. Trains constructing plane equations from every standard geometric specification: a point and a normal, three non-collinear points (computing n = PQ→ × PR→ and diagnosing collinearity when the cross product vanishes), a point and a line not containing it, two intersecting lines, or two parallel distinct lines. Introduces intercept form x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 for sketching planes in the first octant and relates parallel/coincident planes to proportional normal vectors. Enables the learner to construct the equation of any plane from geometric data, read off normal directions, and sketch planar traces and intercepts. Leaves line–plane and plane–plane intersections, dihedral angles, and point-to-plane distances to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Intersections and Angles of Lines and Planes
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes 3D lines and planes (using dot and cross products from earlier ancestors) to analyze relative positions, intersections, and angles between affine subspaces in ℝ³. Solves line–plane intersections by substituting a line's parametric coordinates into a plane's scalar equation, classifying the three mutually exclusive outcomes: unique intersection point (v · n ≠ 0), line parallel and disjoint (v · n = 0 with contradictory constant), or line contained inside the plane (identity 0 = 0). Analyzes pairs of planes as parallel, coincident, or intersecting in a line, training both the geometric construction of the line of intersection (direction d = n_1 × n_2 paired with a single common point found by fixing one coordinate) and direct algebraic elimination. Computes the acute dihedral angle between two intersecting planes via cos θ = |n_1 · n_2| / (‖n_1‖ ‖n_2‖) and the angle φ ∈ [0, π/2] between a line and a plane via sin φ = |v · n| / (‖v‖ ‖n‖), explicitly guarding against the classic mistake of reporting the complementary angle with the normal instead of the angle with the plane. Also constructs planes subject to angular constraints, such as a plane containing a given line and perpendicular to a second plane (n = v × n_2). Enables the learner to resolve all line–plane and plane–plane incidence and angle problems systematically. Leaves metric distance formulas to the distance lessons.

nodes.label: Point-to-Plane, Parallel-Plane, and Point-to-Line Distances
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes 3D lines and planes (together with orthogonal projections and cross products from earlier ancestors) to derive and compute shortest distances and perpendicular feet in space. For a point P_1(x_1, y_1, z_1) and plane ax + by + cz = d with normal n = ⟨a, b, c⟩ and any base point P_0 on the plane, derives the distance as the magnitude of the scalar projection onto n: d(P_1, Π) = |P_0 P_1→ · n| / ‖n‖ = |ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 − d| / √(a² + b² + c²), finds the closest point (foot of the perpendicular) via r_F = r_{P_1} − proj_n(P_0 P_1→) and mirror reflection across the plane, and specializes to the distance between two parallel planes (stressing that both planes must first be scaled to identical normal coefficients) and between a line and a parallel plane. For a point P_1 and a 3D line r(t) = r_0 + t v, develops two complementary distance methods: the parallelogram area/base formula d(P_1, L) = ‖P_0 P_1→ × v‖ / ‖v‖ and the orthogonal decomposition method ‖P_0 P_1→ − proj_v(P_0 P_1→)‖, noting that the projection method simultaneously yields the exact closest point on the line. Enables the learner to compute exact distances, closest points, and reflections for points, lines, and planes in ℝ³. Leaves the distance and common perpendicular between skew lines to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Skew-Line Distance and the Common Perpendicular
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the scalar triple product and point-to-plane/line distances (using skew-line classification from earlier ancestors) to complete the Euclidean metric geometry of lines in ℝ³. Given two skew lines L_1: r_1(t) = P_1 + t d_1 and L_2: r_2(s) = P_2 + s d_2 (so d_1 × d_2 ≠ 0), embeds L_1 and L_2 in two unique parallel planes sharing the common normal n = d_1 × d_2 and projects P_1 P_2→ onto n to derive the shortest distance formula d(L_1, L_2) = |P_1 P_2→ · (d_1 × d_2)| / ‖d_1 × d_2‖—simultaneously interpreting it geometrically as parallelepiped volume divided by base area and verifying that d = 0 recovers coplanarity/intersection. Goes beyond the scalar distance to find the unique closest points Q_1 = r_1(t*) ∈ L_1 and Q_2 = r_2(s*) ∈ L_2 and the equation of the common perpendicular line segment by solving the 2×2 orthogonality system (r_2(s) − r_1(t)) · d_1 = 0 and (r_2(s) − r_1(t)) · d_2 = 0, verifying ‖Q_2 − Q_1‖ against the triple-product formula as an independent check. Enables the learner to compute exact minimum clearance between skew spatial trajectories and locate the endpoints of their common perpendicular. Leaves calculus-based optimization of distance between curved trajectories to Multivariable Calculus.

nodes.label: Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinate Systems
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on quadric surfaces (and assuming polar coordinates in the plane) to introduce the two primary curvilinear coordinate systems in ℝ³. Defines cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z) with conversion formulas x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z (r ≥ 0) and spherical coordinates (ρ, θ, φ) in the standard mathematics convention—radial distance ρ ≥ 0 from the origin, azimuthal angle θ in the xy-plane, and polar angle φ ∈ [0, π] measured downward from the positive z-axis—with x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ, explicitly warning readers about the physics convention that swaps θ and φ. Trains converting points (with careful quadrant checks for θ and φ) and converting canonical surface equations across Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical forms, highlighting how coordinate surfaces simplify key quadrics: circular cylinders (r = a), half-planes (θ = c), spheres centered at the origin (ρ = R), half-cones (φ = φ_0), and circular paraboloids (z = r²). Enables the learner to translate points, regions, and symmetric 3D surfaces fluently among Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates. Leaves volume elements, Jacobians, and triple integrals to Multivariable Calculus.

nodes.label: Vector Triple Products and 3D Vector Identities
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on the scalar triple product to develop advanced 3D vector-algebra identities and vector equations. Proves the vector triple product (BAC–CAB) identity u × (v × w) = (u · w)v − (u · v)w—combining the geometric observation that u × (v × w) lies in the plane spanned by v and w with direct component or aligned-basis verification—and contrasts it with (u × v) × w = (u · w)v − (v · w)u to make non-associativity quantitatively precise. Deduces the Jacobi identity u × (v × w) + v × (w × u) + w × (u × v) = 0 and the Binet–Cauchy identity (a × b) · (c × d) = (a · c)(b · d) − (a · d)(b · c) (generalizing Lagrange's identity). Applies BAC–CAB to simplify nested cross-product expressions, project a vector onto a plane orthogonal to a unit normal n via n × (u × n) = u − (u · n)n, and find the complete family of solutions to the linear cross-product equation a × x = b (showing solvability requires a · b = 0, with general solution x = (b × a)/‖a‖² + t a). Enables the learner to manipulate nested 3D vector products and solve vector cross-product equations algebraically. Leaves Lie algebras and tensor/index notation to higher algebra and physics.
